strengths: AutoSeg addresses a useful problem: discovering and segmenting image-specific categories without user prompts or additional fine-tuning. Decoding clustered BLIP patch embeddings is a promising way to recover objects missed by global captioning.

Comparisons using the same X-Decoder segmentor support BBoost's effectiveness. Table 3 reports 87.1 versus 56.7 VOC mIoU and 30.0 versus 23.4 Cityscapes mIoU against LLaVA-generated vocabularies. Table 1 also shows class-agnostic improvements across all four datasets.

LAVE addresses a real obstacle in evaluating generated category names. Its results are within 0.2–1.1 mIoU of manual mappings across four datasets in Table 4, providing encouraging initial validation.

The manuscript includes diverse datasets, component ablations, implementation parameters, evaluator prompts and pseudocode, and informative success and failure cases. The pretrained models and datasets are identified and cited.
weaknesses: The proposed evaluator has substantive unresolved reliability issues. Section 9.3 relies on the LLM remembering the PASCAL Context and ADE20K vocabularies rather than supplying them; invalid responses become background. The prompts also direct stuff categories to background despite these datasets containing annotated stuff classes. Algorithm 1's exact-match override only partly mitigates this. Aggregate agreement with one manual mapping is reassuring, but mapping accuracy, annotation procedures, and sensitivity to prompting remain unvalidated.

Parameter selection leaves possible evaluation bias unresolved. Section 5.1 optimizes parameters against VOC mIoU without identifying a disjoint tuning split, and the headline results select the best caption-cycle setting for each dataset from Table 2. No variability across stochastic captioning or clustering runs is reported. This particularly weakens conclusions from the small PASCAL Context improvement, 11.7 versus 11.4 mIoU.

Comparisons with ZeroSeg do not clearly establish a common evaluation and supervision protocol. The manuscript does not state that ZeroSeg was reevaluated with LAVE, although Table A7 shows that changing the mapper alone changes AutoSeg's VOC score by 9.6–13.2 points. The role of X-Decoder's pretrained segmentation supervision also needs clearer accounting. Moreover, ZeroSeg already addresses segmentation without supplied category names, limiting the novelty of the task formulation itself.

The central claim of accurate, finer-grained open-ended recognition receives mainly qualitative support. Mapping generated labels back to fixed categories can conceal incorrect fine-grained names, while vocabulary size and dataset-level CLIP similarity do not establish image-specific correctness. A systematic audit of generated labels and masks, including hallucinations and genuinely unannotated categories, is needed to substantiate this contribution.

Several correctable inconsistencies hinder reproduction: Equation 9 specifies independent maximum-IoU assignments rather than the stated Hungarian matching; alignment between the two patch resolutions and handling of the appended positional features before decoding are underspecified; and Table A6 reports 87.1 VOC mIoU for one captioning cycle, whereas Table 2 assigns that score to ten cycles and reports 85.3 for one. These issues are secondary to the evaluation concerns but require clarification.
